Quantum Spin Liquids in Pyrochlore Magnets With Non-Kramers Local Moments

Preprint: APS/123-QED
Tony An Email: t.an@mail.utoronto.ca Affiliation:  Department of Physics, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario M5S 1A7, Canada    Félix Desrochers Affiliation:  Department of Physics, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario M5S 1A7, Canada    Yong Baek Kim Affiliation:  Department of Physics, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario M5S 1A7, Canada
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Numerous experiments on pyrochlore oxides Pr2(Zr, Sn, Hf, Ir)2O7 with non-Kramers Pr3+ ions suggest that they support a quantum spin liquid (QSL) ground state, but the precise nature of the QSL remains unclear. Quantum spin ice with dominant dipolar Ising and smaller quadrupolar transverse exchange interactions is one such candidate, but a dominant inelastic neutron scattering signal suggests that such a picture may not be consistent with experimental results. The microscopic exchange couplings of these compounds are also not known, leaving room for many possible QSL states. In this work, we use Schwinger boson mean-field theory supplemented by a projective symmetry group classification to study possible ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSLs in pyrochlore magnets with dipolar-quadrupolar non-Kramers local moments. We build a mean-field phase diagram and find four QSLs in the frustrated region of parameter space that are consistent with inelastic signals observed in neutron scattering data on Pr2Zr2O7 and Pr2Hf2O7. Among these, two robust QSLs occur in the regime with dominant transverse exchange rather than Ising exchange. We then compute the static and dynamic spin structure factors for these QSL candidates, which can be used to distinguish them in neutron scattering experiments.

I Introduction

Quantum spin liquids (QSLs) are novel quantum paramagnetic states of matter produced by long-range entanglement of interacting spins [49, 69, 34, 73, 11]. QSLs do not order at zero temperature, and they possess fractionalized excitations such as spinons and emergent gauge fields [30, 65, 67, 38, 16, 68, 69, 70]. While a dimer liquid form of QSL is realized in Rydberg atom arrays [62, 55], the discovery of QSL in real materials remains an outstanding challenge in quantum materials research.

Pyrochlore magnets have been considered as possible platforms for QSLs due to the geometric frustration of the pyrochlore lattice (Fig. 1 (a)) [26, 29, 31, 2, 56, 44, 27, 28, 25, 10, 12, 22, 36, 61, 47]. In particular, several promising signatures of QSL behaviour have been observed in pyrochlore rare-earth oxides Pr2​(Zr, Sn, Hf, Ir)2​O7\textrm{Pr}_{2}(\textrm{Zr, Sn, Hf, Ir})_{2}\textrm{O}_{7} [33, 46, 41, 72, 45, 24, 58, 57, 40, 43]. These compounds have the interesting property that the magnetically active Pr3+\textrm{Pr}^{3+} ions are described as a non-Kramers doublet at low energies, which is protected by crystal symmetries, but not by Kramers degeneracy [47]. The non-Kramers doublet is conveniently represented by pseudospins-1/21/2, where the SzS^{z} component transforms as a dipole but the local SxS^{x} and SyS^{y} components transform as quadrupoles [47, 19]. Heat capacity measurements down to 0.350.35 K and DC magnetic susceptibility measurements down to 1.81.8 K show no evidence of a phase transition [33, 46, 72, 45, 58, 43]. Furthermore, neutron scattering experiments in Pr2​Zr2​O7\textrm{Pr}_{2}\textrm{Zr}_{2}\textrm{O}_{7}, Pr2​Hf2​O7\textrm{Pr}_{2}\textrm{Hf}_{2}\textrm{O}_{7}, and Pr2​Sn2​O7\textrm{Pr}_{2}\textrm{Sn}_{2}\textrm{O}_{7} find an inelastic continuum of excitations that could be attributed to fractionalized quasiparticles of a QSL [33, 46, 64, 57, 72, 45].

It has been suggested that the putative QSL in Pr2​Zr2​O7\textrm{Pr}_{2}\textrm{Zr}_{2}\textrm{O}_{7} and Pr2​Hf2​O7\textrm{Pr}_{2}\textrm{Hf}_{2}\textrm{O}_{7} is quantum spin ice (QSI) [33, 60, 57] with dominant dipolar Ising exchange and smaller quadrupolar transverse exchange interactions. The minimal model for QSI is the XXZ model on the pyrochlore lattice

HXXZ=∑⟨i​j⟩[Jz​z​Siz​Sjz−J±​(Si+​Sj−+Si−​Sj+)],H_{\textrm{XXZ}}=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\left[J_{zz}S_{i}^{z}S_{j}^{z}-J_{\pm}(S_{i}^{+}S_{j}^{-}+S_{i}^{-}S_{j}^{+})\right], (1)

where Jz​z>0J_{zz}>0. In classical spin ice (i.e., J±=0J_{\pm}=0), the ground state spin configuration is characterized by the local two-in-two-out constraint, resulting in a macroscopic degeneracy [23]. An excited state with energy gap Jz​zJ_{zz} can be produced by flipping one spin in a particular ground state, creating two “defect tetrahedra” which break the two-in-two-out constraint [23, 9, 13]. Going to the quantum theory in the perturbative regime J±≪Jz​zJ_{\pm}\ll J_{zz}, the action of the transverse operators S±S^{\pm} on the ground state is to create a pair of dispersive spinon-antispinon excitations with an excitation gap on the order of Jz​z/2J_{zz}/2. Formally, QSI can be described by mapping pseudospins to lattice quantum electrodynamics [26, 2, 4, 48, 37]

Siz\displaystyle S^{z}_{i} ∼ℰr​r′\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{E}_{rr^{\prime}} (2a)
Si±\displaystyle S^{\pm}_{i} ∼Φr†​Φr′,\displaystyle\sim\Phi^{\dagger}_{r}\Phi_{r^{\prime}}, (2b)

where ii labels the sites of the pyrochlore lattice and r,r′r,r^{\prime} represent the centers of the tetrahedra sharing the site ii. Here, ℰr​r′\mathcal{E}_{rr^{\prime}} is a lattice electric field and Φr†​Φr′\Phi^{\dagger}_{r}\Phi_{r^{\prime}} represents the creation of a spinon and antispinon pair. Physically, the spinons (“electric charges”) are the quantum analog of the classical defect tetrahedra, while fluctuations of the electric field describe gapless photon excitations of the QSI [26, 2, 4, 48, 37, 51].

In the case of Pr-based pyrochlore magnets, if the ground state is a QSI with the dominant dipolar Ising exchange interaction, only the dipolar Ising moment SzS^{z} or the emergent electric field couples linearly to the neutron spin. On the other hand, the gapped excitations of QSI involve S±S^{\pm} quadrupolar moments and hence they do not couple to neutron spins. Furthermore, although the dual magnetic monopoles or “vison” excitations can couple to neutrons in principle [15], detailed calculations show that such a signal is several orders of magnitude weaker than any contribution from the photons [35]. Hence, neutron scattering is expected to detect the quasielastic low-energy photons while being essentially insensitive to the inelastic signals from gapped spinon excitations and the extremely weak magnetic monopole contribution. On the other hand, neutron scattering in Pr2​Zr2​O7\textrm{Pr}_{2}\textrm{Zr}_{2}\textrm{O}_{7} and Pr2​Hf2​O7\textrm{Pr}_{2}\textrm{Hf}_{2}\textrm{O}_{7} shows significant spectral weight in the inelastic signals, which is inconsistent with the interpretation of the QSI [33, 46, 64, 1, 57]. Interestingly, the inelastic signals show “rod”-like structures in the [h​h​l][hhl] scattering plane [14]. It has been suggested that these inelastic signals may be due to disorder effects [6, 41, 64, 50, 5]. Finally, there is no consensus on the exchange parameters of Pr2​(Zr, Sn, Hf, Ir)2​O7\textrm{Pr}_{2}(\textrm{Zr, Sn, Hf, Ir})_{2}\textrm{O}_{7}, so we have no clear reason to assume that they lie in or even near the spin ice regime in parameter space even without disorder.

Given these facts, we explore alternative quantum spin liquid candidates in pyrochlore magnets with non-Kramers local moments. In this work, instead of considering disorder effects, we investigate the feasibility of quantum spin liquids beyond the quantum spin ice regime, which may explain the dominant inelastic signals in neutron scattering experiments. We study possible ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSLs using Schwinger boson mean-field theory, restricting our attention to QSLs which do not break any space group symmetries or time-reversal symmetry. We use the projective symmetry group (PSG) to classify all such QSLs [66, 63, 39]. We construct the phase diagram and identify the spin liquid candidates that are consistent with the experiments. Among them, the most robust candidates occur in the region where the transverse quadrupolar exchange coupling J±J_{\pm} is dominant. This is a parameter regime where studies on the XXZ model (1) have identified a U⁡(1)U(1) nematic QSL through exact diagonalization and variational calculations [3] and a disordered state with a large nematic susceptibility in pseudo-Majorana fermion functional renormalization group [52]. The ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSLs identified here might be closely competing with these disordered states and may be stabilized by couplings beyond the pristine XXZ model. Finally, we compute the static and dynamic spin structure factors for these candidates to identify their experimental signatures in neutron scattering.

II Model

In praseodymium-based rare-earth pyrochlores, magnetic Pr3+\textrm{Pr}^{3+} ions are located at the shared vertices of neighbouring tetrahedra [22]. Each Pr3+\textrm{Pr}^{3+} has two ff-electrons, and an application of Hund’s rules results in a degenerate J=4J=4 total angular momentum state. A crystal electric field (CEF) with D3​dD_{3d} symmetry splits the J=4J=4 manifold into doublets and singlets. Since there are an even number of electrons, Kramers’ theorem does not apply, so any degeneracy arises from crystal symmetries [47]. Experimentally, it is found that the lowest-lying states form a doublet (i.e., a non-Kramers doublet) and are well separated from the higher CEF states by at least 99 meV [40, 41, 57]. Thus, we are justified in keeping only the non-Kramers doublet degrees of freedom for a low-energy description of the physics. We denote the two degenerate states by |±⟩|\pm\rangle and define pseudospin-1/21/2 operators SS by

Sz\displaystyle S^{z} =12(|+⟩⟨+|−|−⟩⟨−|)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\Big(|+\rangle\langle+|-|-\rangle\langle-|\Big) (3a)
S±\displaystyle S^{\pm} =|±⟩⟨∓|.\displaystyle=|\pm\rangle\langle\mp|. (3b)

Explicitly, the doublet can be written in terms of the standard angular momentum basis |J,m⟩|J,m\rangle with J=4J=4:

|±⟩\displaystyle|\pm\rangle =α|m=±4⟩±β|m=±1⟩−γ|m=∓2⟩\displaystyle=\alpha|m=\pm 4\rangle\pm\beta|m=\pm 1\rangle-\gamma|m=\mp 2\rangle (4)

where α,β,γ∈ℝ\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in\mathbb{R} [53]. The resulting SzS^{z} component of the non-Kramers doublet transforms as a dipole, while the in-plane Sx,SyS^{x},S^{y} components transform as quadrupoles [44].

The pyrochlore lattice is a corner-sharing network of tetrahedra with four sublattices labeled by μ∈{0,1,2,3}\mu\in\{0,1,2,3\}, shown in Fig. 1 (a). The centers of the tetrahedra form a diamond lattice. In global Cartesian coordinates (GCC), we specify the position of the unit cell with the basis vectors

𝒆^1\displaystyle{\bm{\hat{e}}}_{1} =12​(0,1,1)global\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}(0,1,1)_{\textrm{global}} (5a)
𝒆^2\displaystyle{\bm{\hat{e}}}_{2} =12​(1,0,1)global\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}(1,0,1)_{\textrm{global}} (5b)
𝒆^3\displaystyle{\bm{\hat{e}}}_{3} =12​(1,1,0)global.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}(1,1,0)_{\textrm{global}}. (5c)

For notational convenience, we define 𝒆^0=(0,0,0)global{\bm{\hat{e}}}_{0}=(0,0,0)_{\textrm{global}}. We can specify the lattice sites by adding ϵ^μ=12​𝒆^μ\hat{\epsilon}_{\mu}=\frac{1}{2}{\bm{\hat{e}}}_{\mu}, defined as the displacement of the μ\mu sublattice from the 0th0^{\mathrm{th}} sublattice, to the unit cell position. Thus, the sublattice-indexed pyrochlore coordinates are given by

𝒓μ\displaystyle{{\bm{r}}}_{\mu} =r1​𝒆^1+r2​𝒆^2+r3​𝒆^3+ϵ^μ\displaystyle=r_{1}{\bm{\hat{e}}}_{1}+r_{2}{\bm{\hat{e}}}_{2}+r_{3}{\bm{\hat{e}}}_{3}+\hat{\epsilon}_{\mu} (6)
=12​(r2+r3,r1+r3,r1+r2)global+12​𝒆^μ\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}(r_{2}+r_{3},r_{1}+r_{3},r_{1}+r_{2})_{\textrm{global}}+\frac{1}{2}{\bm{\hat{e}}}_{\mu} (7)

The space group of the pyrochlore lattice is generated by the following operators:

  • •

    TiT_{i}: translation by 𝒆^i{\bm{\hat{e}}}_{i} where i∈{1,2,3}i\in\{1,2,3\}.

  • •

    C¯6\overline{C}_{6}: threefold rotation about the [111][111] axis (𝒆^1+𝒆^2+𝒆^3{\bm{\hat{e}}}_{1}+{\bm{\hat{e}}}_{2}+{\bm{\hat{e}}}_{3}) composed with inversion.

  • •

    SS: a “screw” operation defined by fractional translation by ϵ^3=12​𝒆^3\hat{\epsilon}_{3}=\frac{1}{2}{\bm{\hat{e}}}_{3} composed with a π\pi rotation around 𝒆^3{\bm{\hat{e}}}_{3}. [19, 39, 20]

Finally, it is convenient to work in sublattice-dependent local bases to express the orientations of the pseudospins. We attach an orthonormal basis {x^μ,y^μ,z^μ}\{\hat{x}_{\mu},\hat{y}_{\mu},\hat{z}_{\mu}\} to each sublattice μ\mu (expressions given in appendix A). As shown in Fig. 1 (b), these have the property that each z^μ\hat{z}_{\mu} basis vector points out of the “up-pointing” tetrahedra.

Written in the sublattice-dependent local bases, the most general symmetry-allowed nearest-neighbour Hamiltonian for the non-Kramers doublet is

H\displaystyle H =∑⟨i​j⟩[Jz​zSizSjz−J±(Si+Sj−+Si−Sj+)\displaystyle=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\Big[J_{zz}S^{z}_{i}S^{z}_{j}-J_{\pm}(S^{+}_{i}S^{-}_{j}+S^{-}_{i}S^{+}_{j})
+J±⁣±(γi​jSi+Sj++γi​j∗Si−Sj−)],\displaystyle+J_{\pm\pm}(\gamma_{ij}S^{+}_{i}S^{+}_{j}+\gamma_{ij}^{*}S^{-}_{i}S^{-}_{j})\Big], (8)

where i,ji,j denote pyrochlore lattice sites, and γi​j\gamma_{ij} is a bond-dependent phase factor defined in appendix A [44]. We take J±⁣±>0J_{\pm\pm}>0 without loss of generality because its sign can be flipped by a π2\frac{\pi}{2} rotation of each local basis {x^μ,y^μ,z^μ}\{\hat{x}_{\mu},\hat{y}_{\mu},\hat{z}_{\mu}\} about z^μ\hat{z}_{\mu} [17].

III Schwinger Boson Mean-Field Theory and Classification of Spin Liquids

III.1 Schwinger Bosons

We describe prospective QSLs using the Schwinger boson construction, in which the pseudospins (8) at pyrochlore site ii are expressed as

Sia\displaystyle S^{a}_{i} =12​∑α​βbi​α†​[σa]α​β​bi​β\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha\beta}b^{\dagger}_{i\alpha}[\sigma^{a}]_{\alpha\beta}b_{i\beta} (9)

where a∈{x,y,z}a\in\{x,y,z\} and σa\sigma^{a} are the Pauli matrices. The operators bi​αb_{i\alpha} satisfy the bosonic commutation relations [bi​α,bj​β†]=δi​j​δα​β[b_{i\alpha},b^{\dagger}_{j\beta}]=\delta_{ij}\delta_{\alpha\beta}. The Schwinger bosons physically represent the fractionalized excitations of the QSL, which we refer to as spinons. If we impose the local constraint

ni=∑αbi​α†​bi​α=κn_{i}=\sum_{\alpha}b^{\dagger}_{i\alpha}b_{i\alpha}=\kappa (10)

with κ=1\kappa=1, we obtain a faithful representation of the original pseudospin-1/21/2 Hilbert space [36, 63]. In the mean-field theory, this constraint is relaxed to only be satisfied on average

⟨ni⟩=κ\langle n_{i}\rangle=\kappa (11)

for all sites ii. We will also treat κ\kappa as a continuous positive parameter, which gives us control over the size of quantum effects. Taking κ→∞\kappa\to\infty recovers the classical limit, and κ<1\kappa<1 corresponds to larger quantum fluctuations. In the current work, we focus on small κ≪1\kappa\ll 1 to obtain all the competing QSLs, and comment on what is expected in the physical κ=1\kappa=1 limit later in sections IV.2 and V [42]. As κ\kappa increases, magnetic order may develop in some parts of the phase diagram, signaled by the closing of the spinon gap and condensation of Schwinger bosons [63, 21, 39].

III.2 Mean-Field Decoupling

We define 8 bond operators as follows:

χ^i​j\displaystyle\hat{\chi}_{ij} =∑αbi​α†​bj​α\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha}b^{\dagger}_{i\alpha}b_{j\alpha} (12a)
E^i​ja\displaystyle\hat{E}^{a}_{ij} =∑α​βbi​α†​[σa]α​β​bj​β\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\beta}b^{\dagger}_{i\alpha}[\sigma^{a}]_{\alpha\beta}b_{j\beta} (12b)
Δ^i​j\displaystyle\hat{\Delta}_{ij} =∑α​βbi​α​[i​σy]α​β​bj​β\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\beta}b_{i\alpha}[i\sigma^{y}]_{\alpha\beta}b_{j\beta} (12c)
D^i​ja\displaystyle\hat{D}^{a}_{ij} =∑α​βbi​α​[i​σy​σa]α​β​bj​β,\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\beta}b_{i\alpha}[i\sigma^{y}\sigma^{a}]_{\alpha\beta}b_{j\beta}, (12d)

where a∈{x,y,z}a\in\{x,y,z\}. The operators χ^,E→^\hat{\chi},\hat{\vec{E}} are known as the singlet/triplet hopping, and Δ^,D→^\hat{\Delta},\hat{\vec{D}} are known as the singlet/triplet pairing. After replacing the pseudospins with Schwinger bosons, we write the Hamiltonian in the form

H\displaystyle H =−∑⟨i​j⟩𝑩i​j†ξi​j𝑩i​j\displaystyle=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\bm{B}_{ij}^{\dagger}\xi_{ij}\bm{B}_{ij} (13)

𝑩i​j\displaystyle\bm{B}_{ij} =(χ^,E^x,E^y,E^z,Δ^,D^x,D^y,D^z)i​j⊺\displaystyle=(\hat{\chi},\hat{E}^{x},\hat{E}^{y},\hat{E}^{z},\hat{\Delta},\hat{D}^{x},\hat{D}^{y},\hat{D}^{z})_{ij}^{\intercal} (14)

and ξi​j∈ℝ8×8\xi_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{8\times 8} is a real symmetric matrix to ensure HH is Hermitian. The decoupling matrix ξi​j\xi_{ij} is not determined uniquely, but we choose it to be positive-definite for reasons explained in appendices D and E. From Eq. (13), we are led to the mean-field decoupling

HMF\displaystyle H_{\textrm{MF}} =−∑⟨i​j⟩(𝑩i​j†ξi​j𝓐i​j+𝓐i​j†ξi​j𝑩i​j−𝓐i​j†ξi​j𝓐i​j),\displaystyle=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}(\bm{B}_{ij}^{\dagger}\xi_{ij}\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{ij}+\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}^{\dagger}_{ij}\xi_{ij}\bm{B}_{ij}-\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}^{\dagger}_{ij}\xi_{ij}\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{ij}), (15)

𝓐i​j\displaystyle\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{ij} =(χ,Ex,Ey,Ez,Δ,Dx,Dy,Dz)i​j⊺.\displaystyle=(\chi,E^{x},E^{y},E^{z},\Delta,D^{x},D^{y},D^{z})_{ij}^{\intercal}. (16)

Regardless of the choice of decoupling, the mean-field Hamiltonian can be rewritten in the form

The matrices ui​jhu_{ij}^{h} and ui​jpu_{ij}^{p} are parameterized by complex numbers a,b,c,da,b,c,d as follows:

ui​jh\displaystyle u^{h}_{ij} =ai​jh​𝟙𝟚×𝟚+𝕓𝕚​𝕛𝕙​σ𝕩+𝕔𝕚​𝕛𝕙​σ𝕪+𝕕𝕚​𝕛𝕙​σ𝕫\displaystyle=a^{h}_{ij}\openone_{2\times 2}+b^{h}_{ij}\sigma^{x}+c_{ij}^{h}\sigma^{y}+d_{ij}^{h}\sigma^{z} (18a)

III.3 Projective Symmetry Group Classification

In this section, we use the projective symmetry group (PSG) to classify the different mean-field ansätze. We are interested in ansätze which break no space group symmetries or time-reversal symmetry. However, the Schwinger boson representation contains a U⁡(1)U(1) gauge redundancy because the pseudospin operators (9) are invariant under the transformation

G:𝒃j↦ei​ϕ​[j]​𝒃jG:\bm{b}_{j}\mapsto e^{i\phi[j]}\bm{b}_{j} (19)

Two ansätze which differ by a gauge transformation of the form (19) are therefore physically equivalent [66, 67, 63]. The correct way to implement symmetry operations is via the gauge-enriched operations 𝒪~=G𝒪∘𝒪\tilde{{\mathcal{O}}}=G_{\mathcal{O}}\circ{\mathcal{O}}, where 𝒪{\mathcal{O}} is an element of the pyrochlore lattice space group [66, 63]. Explicitly, the action of 𝒪~\tilde{{\mathcal{O}}} is

𝒪~:𝒃j↦ei​ϕ𝒪​[𝒪⁡(j)]​U𝒪†​𝒃𝒪⁡(j),\tilde{{\mathcal{O}}}:\bm{b}_{j}\mapsto e^{i\phi_{\mathcal{O}}[{\mathcal{O}}(j)]}U_{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}\bm{b}_{{\mathcal{O}}(j)}, (20)

where U𝒪U_{\mathcal{O}} is a 2×22\times 2 unitary matrix representation of the space group operation. Similarly, the action of the gauge-enriched time reversal operation is

𝒯~:𝒃j↦ei​ϕ𝒯​[j]​𝒦​U𝒯†​𝒃j\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{T}}:\bm{b}_{j}\mapsto e^{i\phi_{\mathcal{T}}[j]}\mathcal{K}U_{\mathcal{T}}^{\dagger}\bm{b}_{j} (21)

with 𝒦\mathcal{K} being the complex conjugation operator and U𝒯U_{\mathcal{T}} is a 2×22\times 2 unitary matrix [39]. Explicit expressions for U𝒪U_{\mathcal{O}} and U𝒯U_{\mathcal{T}} are derived in appendix B; here we simply list the results

UT1=UT2=UT3\displaystyle U_{T_{1}}=U_{T_{2}}=U_{T_{3}} =𝟙𝟚×𝟚\displaystyle=\openone_{2\times 2} (22a)
UC¯6\displaystyle U_{\overline{C}_{6}} =(ω∗00ω)\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}\omega^{*}&0\\ 0&\omega\end{pmatrix} (22b)
US\displaystyle U_{S} =(0ω∗ω0)\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}0&\omega^{*}\\ \omega&0\end{pmatrix} (22c)
U𝒯\displaystyle U_{\mathcal{T}} =(0110)\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix} (22d)

where ω=e2​π​i/3\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}. The group generated by the gauge-enriched operations 𝒪~\tilde{{\mathcal{O}}} and 𝒯~\tilde{\mathcal{T}} is known as the projective symmetry group (PSG) [66, 63, 39]. Demanding that the mean-field Hamiltonian is invariant under the PSG elements puts constraints on the allowed mean-field ansätze. Ansätze that cannot be transformed into each other via a pure gauge transformation (19) belong to different PSG classes, meaning they describe different QSLs [66, 63].

The subgroup of the PSG corresponding to pure gauge transformations associated with the identity operation 𝒪=id{\mathcal{O}}=\mathrm{id} is known as the invariant gauge group [66, 63]. The invariant gauge group corresponds to the emergent gauge structure of the resulting QSLs [66, 67]. In this paper, we only consider the ℤ2={ei​π​n|n∈{0,1}}\mathbb{Z}_{2}=\{e^{i\pi n}|n\in\{0,1\}\} invariant gauge group, thus restricting our study to ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetric bosonic QSLs.

Previous work on ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Schwinger boson mean-field theory has identified 1616 possible ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetric bosonic QSLs, with the phase factors ϕG\phi_{G} given by

ϕT1​(𝒓μ)\displaystyle\phi_{T_{1}}({{\bm{r}}}_{\mu}) =0\displaystyle=0 (23a)
ϕT2​(𝒓μ)\displaystyle\phi_{T_{2}}({{\bm{r}}}_{\mu}) =n1​π​r1\displaystyle=n_{1}\pi r_{1} (23b)
ϕT3​(𝒓μ)\displaystyle\phi_{T_{3}}({{\bm{r}}}_{\mu}) =n1​π​(r1+r2)\displaystyle=n_{1}\pi(r_{1}+r_{2}) (23c)

+n1​π​r1​(r2+r3)\displaystyle+n_{1}\pi r_{1}(r_{2}+r_{3}) (23d)
ϕS​(𝒓μ)\displaystyle\phi_{S}({{\bm{r}}}_{\mu}) =[(−1)δμ=1,2,3​n1+nS​T12+δμ=2​nC¯6​S]​π\displaystyle=\left[(-1)^{\delta_{\mu=1,2,3}}\frac{n_{1}+{n_{ST_{1}}}}{2}+\delta_{\mu=2}{n_{\overline{C}_{6}S}}\right]\pi
+(n1​δμ=1,2+nS​T1)​π​r1\displaystyle+(n_{1}\delta_{\mu=1,2}+{n_{ST_{1}}})\pi r_{1}
+(n1​δμ=2+nS​T1)​π​r2+n1​π​r3​δμ=1,2\displaystyle+(n_{1}\delta_{\mu=2}+{n_{ST_{1}}})\pi r_{2}+n_{1}\pi r_{3}\delta_{\mu=1,2}
+12​n1​π​(r1+r2)​(r1+r2+1)\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}n_{1}\pi(r_{1}+r_{2})(r_{1}+r_{2}+1) (23e)

where n1,nC¯6​S,nS​T1,nC¯6n_{1},n_{\overline{C}_{6}S},n_{ST_{1}},n_{\overline{C}_{6}} are all either 00 or 11 [39]. Even though the PSG solution is the same as the effective spin-1/21/2 [39] and dipolar-octupolar cases [20], the structure of the allowed mean-field ansätze will be different because of the pseudospin transformation matrices U𝒪U_{\mathcal{O}} and U𝒯U_{\mathcal{T}}. Following [39], we shift the first Brillouin zone 𝒒↦𝒒−(π,π,π){{\bm{q}}}\mapsto{{\bm{q}}}-(\pi,\pi,\pi) for the PSG classes with nS​T1=1{n_{ST_{1}}}=1, which is equivalent to a gauge transformation and does not affect physical quantities on the spin level.

The PSG classes with n1=1n_{1}=1 have an enlarged unit cell because the translations T2T_{2} and T3T_{3} act projectively, which means that the translation-invariance of the ansatz is realized after projecting from the Schwinger boson Hilbert space down to the physical spin Hilbert space. We do not consider these classes in this work. There is no physical reason to exclude them, but only considering n1=0n_{1}=0 simplifies the calculations and the presentation of results. We therefore label the different n1=0n_{1}=0 PSG classes using the notation (nC¯6​S​nS​T1​nC¯6)(n_{\overline{C}_{6}S}n_{ST_{1}}n_{\overline{C}_{6}}).

III.4 Generalized Self-Consistent Equations

The self-consistent equations for our ansatz are determined by extremizing the mean-field energy ⟨HM​F⟩\langle H_{MF}\rangle with respect to the amplitudes 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} and the Lagrange multiplier λ\lambda. For the latter, we obtain the average occupation constraint (11);

∂⟨HMF⟩∂λ=0\displaystyle\frac{\partial\langle H_{\textrm{MF}}\rangle}{\partial\lambda}=0 ⇔⟨ni⟩=κ.\displaystyle\iff\langle n_{i}\rangle=\kappa. (24)

Assuming that each bond of the ansatz is independent and that ξ\xi is invertible, minimizing the mean-field energy with respect to each mean-field amplitude results in the self-consistent equations

⟨𝑩i​j⟩\displaystyle\langle\bm{B}_{ij}\rangle =𝓐i​j\displaystyle=\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{ij} (25)

for every bond (i,j)(i,j). The approach taken in previous work was to search for a subset of solutions to (25) that respected the PSG constraints [63, 54, 20].

However, our insistence that the ansatz respects the PSG constraints means this approach does not hold in all situations. When we impose the PSG constraints, the bonds are no longer independent. In fact, we only need to specify the MF parameters on one bond to fully determine their values on all other bonds. Thus, the derivation of (25) is modified, as described in more detail in appendix E. We find a set of generalized self-consistent equations of the form

⟨𝑩i0,j0⟩\displaystyle\langle\bm{B}_{i_{0},j_{0}}\rangle =ℳ​𝓐i0,j0\displaystyle=\mathcal{M}\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{i_{0},j_{0}} (26)

where the matrix ℳ∈ℝ8×8\mathcal{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{8\times 8} is determined by the decoupling matrix ξ\xi and the PSG. We note that this equation only holds for the reference bond (i0,j0)=(𝟎0,𝟎1)(i_{0},j_{0})=(\bm{0}_{0},\bm{0}_{1}); the values of ⟨𝑩i​j⟩\langle\bm{B}_{ij}\rangle and 𝓐i​j\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{ij} for other bonds are fully determined by the MF values on the reference bond and the PSG. For simple choices of the decoupling, it can happen that ℳ=𝟙𝟠×𝟠\mathcal{M}=\openone_{8\times 8}, recovering the usual result (25). We find that it is not possible to choose such a decoupling for our Hamiltonian (8) (appendix D), so the self-consistent equations always take a slightly more complicated form for the amplitudes ExE^{x}, EyE^{y}, DxD^{x}, and DyD^{y}.

IV Results

IV.1 Phase Diagram

We compute the mean-field phase diagrams for κ=0.1\kappa=0.1 and Jz​z2+J±2+J±⁣±2=1J_{zz}^{2}+J_{\pm}^{2}+J_{\pm\pm}^{2}=1 with J±<0J_{\pm}<0 and J±⁣±>0J_{\pm\pm}>0, which are presented in Fig. 1 (c) and (d). We chose a small value of κ\kappa to obtain all the competing QSL phases, since some QSLs may be unstable to magnetic ordering as κ\kappa increases. We discuss this further in sections IV.2 and V. We also chose J±<0J_{\pm}<0 to explore the region of the parameter space with frustrated in-plane interactions, where QSLs are more likely to arise. Indeed, numerical studies have shown that the region J±>0J_{\pm}>0 for J±≥Jz​z=0.05J_{\pm}\geq J_{zz}=0.05 and Jz​z>0J_{zz}>0 favours an in-plane pseudospin ferromagnetic order, while the region J±>0J_{\pm}>0 for Jz​z<0J_{zz}<0 favours in-plane or Ising-type pseudospin ferromagnetic order [2, 32, 27, 28, 59, 3, 52, 17]. We parameterize the exchange couplings by

Jz​z=sin⁡θ​cos⁡ϕ,J±=−cos⁡θ,J±⁣±=sin⁡θ​sin⁡ϕJ_{zz}=\sin\theta\cos\phi,\ J_{\pm}=-\cos\theta,\ J_{\pm\pm}=\sin\theta\sin\phi (27)

where θ∈(0,π2)\theta\in(0,\frac{\pi}{2}) and ϕ∈(0,π)\phi\in(0,\pi). As such, ϕ<π/2\phi<\pi/2 corresponds to Jz​z>0J_{zz}>0 while ϕ>π/2\phi>\pi/2 corresponds to Jz​z<0J_{zz}<0.

Since we have specialized to n1=0n_{1}=0, there are at most 88 PSG classes to consider. For the range of parameters we studied, we found that certain PSG classes had identical mean-field ansätze in the regime of interest. Namely, the ansätze (100)(100) and (110)(110) were identical, as well (101)(101) and (111)(111), reducing the number of PSG classes to 66. Strictly speaking, ansätze belonging to distinct PSG classes are still inequivalent, but we will treat them as the same since the resulting observables are the same. We expect this degeneracy to be lifted upon inclusion of other interactions or next-nearest neighbour terms in the mean-field ansätze.

We find that the lowest-energy state is often accompanied by a closely competing state, with a relative difference in mean-field energy on the order of 10−410^{-4} to 10−210^{-2}. Thus, we show both the lowest- and second-lowest-energy states in Fig. 1 (c) and (d), respectively. We find that (000)(000) is favoured in the antiferromagnetic (AFM) Ising (Jz​z=1J_{zz}=1) and J±⁣±=1J_{\pm\pm}=1 limits, (101)(101) is favoured in the AFM XY limit (J±=−1J_{\pm}=-1), and (010)(010) is favoured in the ferromagnetic (FM) Ising (Jz​z=−1J_{zz}=-1) limit. The transition from (000)(000) to (101)(101) occurs roughly when θ<π/4\theta<\pi/4, which is when J±J_{\pm} becomes the dominant coupling.

We point out the phase transition near the antiferromagnetic Heisenberg point J±/Jz​z=−12J_{\pm}/J_{zz}=-\frac{1}{2}, J±⁣±=0J_{\pm\pm}=0 where Jz​z>0J_{zz}>0, which is expected at the classical level [59, 47]. Cluster-variational and pseudo-Majorana fermion functional renormalization group studies of the XXZ model on the pyrochlore lattice also support a phase transition to a magnetically disordered state there as well [3, 52], which supports our finding. Figure 1 (d) shows that the phases (011)(011), (100)(100), and (001)(001) are the second lowest energy phases competing with (000)(000), (101)(101), and (010)(010) respectively. There is also a small region where (101)(101) has the second lowest energy compared to (000)(000). Excluding that small region, the pairs of lowest- and second-lowest-energy PSG classes have the same non-vanishing mean-field parameters ah,…,dh,ap,…,dpa^{h},\ldots,d^{h},a^{p},\ldots,d^{p}, defined in Eqs. (18a-18b). However, they can still have distinct physical properties since they have different PSG parameters nC¯6​S,nS​T1,nC¯6{n_{\overline{C}_{6}S}},{n_{ST_{1}}},{n_{\overline{C}_{6}}} which govern the spatial structure of the ansätze. Examples of this are shown in the next two sections.

IV.2 Distinguishing Properties of Different PSG Classes

Here we describe the different phases occurring in Fig. 1 in more detail. For the rest of this work, all computations for a given PSG class are done using the self-consistent mean-field ansätze at the points marked by the ×\times’s in Fig. 1 (c) and (d), and given in table 1.

The spinon dispersions of the six PSG classes are shown in Fig. 2. As discussed in section IV.1, we chose κ=0.1\kappa=0.1 so that all QSLs are gapped. However, we note that (000)(000) has a significantly larger bandwidth and smaller energy gap than the other classes, indicating its susceptibility to Schwinger boson condensation. In fact, for κ≈0.14\kappa\approx 0.14, the class (000)(000) is condensed throughout the entire phase diagram. The minimum of its dispersion occurs at 𝒒=0{{\bm{q}}}=0, consistent with the ordering wave vector expected from the classical phase diagram [47, 17, 71]. The smaller bandwidth and larger gap of the other PSG classes make them more resistant to condensation, making them more likely to persist at higher values of κ\kappa.

The different PSG classes are distinguishable through their local frame equal-time spin structure factors 𝒮LFα​β​(𝒒)\mathcal{S}^{\alpha\beta}_{\textrm{LF}}({{\bm{q}}}). These are defined by the spin-spin correlations

𝒮LFα​β​(𝒒)\displaystyle\mathcal{S}^{\alpha\beta}_{\textrm{LF}}({{\bm{q}}}) =1Nuc​∑𝒓μ,𝒓ν′ei​𝒒⋅(𝒓μ−𝒓ν′)​⟨S𝒓μα​S𝒓ν′β⟩\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N_{\textrm{uc}}}\sum_{{{\bm{r}}}_{\mu},{{\bm{r}}}^{\prime}_{\nu}}e^{i{{\bm{q}}}\cdot({{\bm{r}}}_{\mu}-{{\bm{r}}}^{\prime}_{\nu})}\langle S_{{{\bm{r}}}_{\mu}}^{\alpha}S_{{{\bm{r}}}^{\prime}_{\nu}}^{\beta}\rangle (28)

and are shown in Fig. 3. The qualitative behaviour of 𝒮LFα​β​(𝒒)\mathcal{S}^{\alpha\beta}_{\textrm{LF}}({{\bm{q}}}) can be understood by looking at which mean-field amplitudes are nonzero after solving the generalized self-consistent equations (26). The simplest are (101)(101) and (100)(100), which only have a nonzero singlet pairing Δ\Delta everywhere in the phase diagram. Since all triplet terms vanish, this gives them an emergent S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry, so 𝒮LFx​x=𝒮LFy​y=𝒮LFz​z\mathcal{S}^{xx}_{\textrm{LF}}=\mathcal{S}^{yy}_{\textrm{LF}}=\mathcal{S}^{zz}_{\textrm{LF}} for these two PSG classes. The intensity of 𝒮LF\mathcal{S}_{\textrm{LF}} has has maxima at nonzero 𝒒{{\bm{q}}} ([002][002] and symmetry-related points), indicating antiferromagnetic correlations. This is consistent with the fact that the antiferromagnetic J±J_{\pm} is the dominant coupling when (101)(101) and (100)(100) have the lowest energy.

When Jz​z>0J_{zz}>0, the classes (000)(000) and (011)(011) have nonzero singlet hopping χ\chi and triplet pairing DzD^{z}. Since all the xx and yy triplet terms vanish, there is an emergent U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry that ensures 𝒮LFx​x=𝒮LFy​y\mathcal{S}^{xx}_{\textrm{LF}}=\mathcal{S}^{yy}_{\textrm{LF}}. The intensity of 𝒮LFz​z\mathcal{S}^{zz}_{\textrm{LF}} has maxima at nonzero 𝒒{{\bm{q}}} ([002][002] and symmetry-related points), which is consistent with the antiferromagnetic Jz​zJ_{zz} coupling.

On the other hand, the self-consistent ansätze in the Jz​z<0J_{zz}<0 region for (000)(000) and (011)(011) have nonzero χ,Dx,Dy\chi,D^{x},D^{y}, which include xx and yy triplet mean-field amplitudes. The same is true for (010)(010) and (001)(001). As such, there is no emergent symmetry in these phases, and the spin-spin correlations are different for each component. In contrast to the previous two classes, the intensity of 𝒮LFz​z\mathcal{S}^{zz}_{\textrm{LF}} has a maximum at [000][000], which is consistent with the ferromagnetic Jz​zJ_{zz} coupling. Figure 3 shows that 𝒮LFz​z\mathcal{S}^{zz}_{\textrm{LF}} is significantly stronger than the in-plane correlations for (010)(010) and (001)(001), but weaker than the in-plane correlations for (000)(000) and (011)(011).

IV.3 Dynamic Spin Structure Factor

The observable we are primarily interested in is the dynamic spin structure factor (DSSF) 𝒮\mathcal{S}, which is directly related to the inelastic neutron scattering cross section [36, 7]. The quadrupolar SxS^{x} and SyS^{y} do not couple to the neutron’s spin [15], so neutron scattering only probes correlations between SzS^{z}. The resulting DSSF is

𝒮⁡(𝒒,ω)\displaystyle\mathcal{S}({{\bm{q}}},\omega) =∑μ​ν(z^μ⋅z^ν−(z^μ⋅𝒒)​(z^ν⋅𝒒)|𝒒|2)​𝒮LF,μ​νz​z​(𝒒,ω)\displaystyle=\sum_{\mu\nu}\left(\hat{z}_{\mu}\cdot\hat{z}_{\nu}-\frac{(\hat{z}_{\mu}\cdot{{\bm{q}}})(\hat{z}_{\nu}\cdot{{\bm{q}}})}{|{{\bm{q}}}|^{2}}\right)\mathcal{S}^{zz}_{\textrm{LF},\mu\nu}({{\bm{q}}},\omega) (29)

where the prefactor includes the transverse projector and the rotation from the pseudospin local frames to the global frame in Cartesian coordinates. The local frame DSSF is defined as

𝒮LF,μ​να​β​(𝒒,ω)\displaystyle\mathcal{S}^{\alpha\beta}_{\textrm{LF},\mu\nu}({{\bm{q}}},\omega) =12​π​Nuc​∫d​t​ei​𝒒⋅(𝒓μ−𝒓ν′)+i​ω​t​⟨S𝒓μα​(t)​S𝒓ν′β​(0)⟩.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi N_{\textrm{uc}}}\int\mathrm{d}te^{i{{\bm{q}}}\cdot({{\bm{r}}}_{\mu}-{{\bm{r}}}^{\prime}_{\nu})+i\omega t}\langle S_{{{\bm{r}}}_{\mu}}^{\alpha}(t)S_{{{\bm{r}}}^{\prime}_{\nu}}^{\beta}(0)\rangle. (30)

Note that the local frame equal-time spin structure factor (28) is obtained from Eq. (30) by integrating over ω\omega.

We can gain some qualitative insight by first computing the equal-time structure factor (relevant for energy-integrated neutron scattering experiments)

𝒮ET​(𝒒)=∫𝒮⁡(𝒒,ω)​𝑑ω.\mathcal{S}_{\textrm{ET}}({{\bm{q}}})=\int\mathcal{S}({{\bm{q}}},\omega)\mathrm{d}\omega. (31)

We find a high-intensity “rod” pattern (Fig. 4 (a)) for the PSG classes (000)(000) and (011)(011) only when Jz​z>0J_{zz}>0. They also occur for the PSG classes (101)(101) and (100)(100) for both signs of Jz​zJ_{zz}. The high-intensity rods in the [h​h​l][hhl] plane resemble the washed-out pinch point structure observed in experiments [33, 46, 64]. Such rods appear in single tetrahedron calculations of the equal-time structure factor [14]. On the other hand, we find low-intensity rods (Fig. 4 (b)) for (000)(000) and (011)(011) when Jz​z<0J_{zz}<0, as well as for (010)(010) and (001)(001) regardless of the sign of Jz​zJ_{zz}. Since the high-intensity pattern better matches what is experimentally observed, we restrict our attention to the phases (000),(011)(000),(011) (in the region Jz​z>0J_{zz}>0), and (101),(100)(101),(100) for the rest of this work.

We show the full dynamic spin structure factor and lower/upper edges of the two-spinon continuum along a high symmetry path in the first Brillouin zone in Fig. 5. The two-spinon continuum at 𝒒{{\bm{q}}} is defined as the energy interval

min𝒌∈BZ⁡(ω𝒌+ω𝒒−𝒌)≤ω≤max𝒌∈BZ⁡(ω𝒌+ω𝒒−𝒌),\min_{{{\bm{k}}}\in\textrm{BZ}}(\omega_{{\bm{k}}}+\omega_{{{\bm{q}}}-{{\bm{k}}}})\leq\omega\leq\max_{{{\bm{k}}}\in\textrm{BZ}}(\omega_{{\bm{k}}}+\omega_{{{\bm{q}}}-{{\bm{k}}}}), (32)

where ω𝒌\omega_{{\bm{k}}} is the spinon dispersion (see Fig. 2). Physically, a neutron that excites two spinons and is scattered with momentum transfer 𝒒{{\bm{q}}} must transfer an energy ω\omega that lies within the two-spinon continuum, at least at the mean-field level with non-interacting spinons. The DSSF is therefore 00 outside the two-spinon continuum. The DSSFs of most candidates include a relatively flat feature where most of the spectral weight is concentrated, which is expected from the flatness of the spinon bands as shown in Fig. 2. These DSSFs are broadly consistent with the inelastic signal observed in experiments, but the resolution of currently available instruments may not be fine enough to show any of the detailed features in Fig. 5. Interestingly, the DSSF for (000)(000) has a near-uniform 𝒒{{\bm{q}}}-dependence, which we attribute to the vanishing of the mean-field amplitudes DxD^{x} and DyD^{y} after reaching self-consistency, causing cp=0c^{p}=0 (as defined in Eq. 18b). In fact, cp≠0c^{p}\neq 0 when Jz​z<0J_{zz}<0 for (000)(000), and a nontrivial 𝒒{{\bm{q}}}-dependence in the DSSF is seen.

We also show energy cuts of 𝒮⁡(𝒒,ω)\mathcal{S}({{\bm{q}}},\omega) integrated over energy windows (ω¯−δ​ω,ω¯+δ​ω)(\overline{\omega}-\delta\omega,\overline{\omega}+\delta\omega) in the [h​h​l][hhl] plane in Fig. 6. Together, the windows cover the entire two-spinon continuum. Due to the flat features seen in the momentum-resolved DSSF (Fig. 5), the energy window ω¯\overline{\omega} centered around the flat feature will have the highest intensity. The cleanest realization of the rod structure occurs in the higher energy windows of (000)(000), but it can also be seen in the other candidates. Some energy-integrated windows display significant modulation of the rods, which is similar to what has been observed in Pr2​Hf2​O7\textrm{Pr}_{2}\textrm{Hf}_{2}\textrm{O}_{7} [57].

V Discussion

We investigated possible QSL phases beyond the quantum spin ice regime for pyrochlore oxides with non-Kramers magnetic ions. Local moments are described by pseudospin degrees of freedom consisting of dipolar Ising and quadrupolar XY moments. We used a Schwinger boson mean-field theory and the corresponding projective symmetry group to classify ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} quantum spin liquids on the pyrochlore lattice with non-Kramers ions. By constructing a mean-field phase diagram, we identified four candidate QSLs in the frustrated region of parameter space that show a high intensity rod structure in the [h​h​l][hhl] plane, consistent with the inelastic signal in neutron scattering experiments [33, 46, 57]. Certain energy-integrated windows of the dynamic spin structure factor show a modulated rod structure that is reminiscent of the features in neutron scattering experiments.

Using our PSG classification scheme, the lowest energy ansätze that are consistent with experiment are the states (000)(000) and (101)(101), but it is important to keep in mind that (011)(011) and (100)(100) are closely competing states in the relevant parameter space. These states can be distinguished by the intensity patterns in their dynamical spin structure factors.

In Schwinger boson mean-field theory, we use κ\kappa, the average boson occupation number per site, as a control parameter for quantum fluctuations. Smaller κ\kappa means larger quantum fluctuations. In order to obtain all the competing QSL phases, we set κ=0.1\kappa=0.1 in the mean-field phase diagram, which is much smaller than the physical value of κ=1\kappa=1. Upon increasing κ\kappa, we find that the phase (000)(000) is much more susceptible to Schwinger boson condensation than the other three phases because of its large spinon bandwidth and small excitation gap at 𝒒=0{{\bm{q}}}=0. This suggests that the region covered by (000)(000) becomes magnetically ordered (with 𝒒=0{{\bm{q}}}=0 ordering wave vector) for realistic values of κ\kappa, unlike (101)(101) and (100)(100) which are more robust due to their narrow and relatively flat spinon bands, and large excitation gap. In this sense, (101)(101) and (100)(100) are stronger ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSL candidates.

Our phase diagram shows that the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} quantum spin liquids (101)(101) and (100)(100) are energetically favoured when J±J_{\pm} is the dominant coupling. Interestingly, numerical studies of the XXZ model (1) using cluster-variational and pseudo-Majorana fermion functional renormalization group calculations also find a transition to a disordered state past the antiferromagnetic Heisenberg point J±/Jz​z<−12J_{\pm}/J_{zz}<-\frac{1}{2} where Jz​z>0J_{zz}>0 [3, 52]. This supports the possibility that a quantum spin liquid could occur when |J±||J_{\pm}| becomes comparable to or larger than |Jz​z||J_{zz}|. Thus, it is possible that (101)(101) and (100)(100) are among several competing QSL phases in this region of parameter space.

The non-Kramers doublet can be split by crystalline disorder or local strain because its degeneracy is protected only by crystalline symmetries, not by time-reversal symmetry. Previous work indicates that this plays an important role in Pr2​Zr2​O7\textrm{Pr}_{2}\textrm{Zr}_{2}\textrm{O}_{7} physics and could explain the inelastic neutron scattering signal [41, 64, 50, 5]. It will be important to precisely determine the exchange couplings Jz​z,J±,J±⁣±J_{zz},J_{\pm},J_{\pm\pm} to reliably assess the effects of disorder. At the moment, these parameters are mostly unknown. In the context of Schwinger boson theory, future work could investigate the effects of disorder on candidate QSL phases. On the other hand, our analysis may be more directly applicable to Pr2​Hf2​O7\textrm{Pr}_{2}\textrm{Hf}_{2}\textrm{O}_{7}, which is claimed to have minimal disorder [57].

Appendix A Microscopic Model

Starting from Hund’s rules, an f2f^{2} state has total spin S=1S=1 and orbital angular momentum L=5L=5, leading to a total angular momentum of J=4J=4. Decomposing the 9-dimensional representation ΓJ=4\Gamma_{J=4} of S​O​(3)SO(3) in terms of irreducible representations of the double group of D3​dD_{3d}, we find

ΓJ=4=2​A1​g⊕A2​g⊕3​Eg\Gamma_{J=4}=2A_{1g}\oplus A_{2g}\oplus 3E_{g} (33)

in terms of standard Mulliken notation [8]. The two-dimensional irreducible representation EgE_{g} forms the non-Kramers doublet, with an explicit construction given in Eq. (4) [47].

The local basis vectors for the four sublattices of the pyrochlore lattice are shown in table 2. The bond-dependent phase factor γi​j=γ𝒓μ,𝒓ν′\gamma_{ij}=\gamma_{{{\bm{r}}}_{\mu},{{\bm{r}}}^{\prime}_{\nu}} depends only on the sublattice indices (μ,ν)(\mu,\nu), and is defined by

γμ​ν\displaystyle\gamma_{\mu\nu} =(01ωω210ω2ωωω201ω2ω10)\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&\omega&\omega^{2}\\ 1&0&\omega^{2}&\omega\\ \omega&\omega^{2}&0&1\\ \omega^{2}&\omega&1&0\end{pmatrix} (34)

where ω=e2​π​i/3\omega=e^{2\pi i/3} [44].

Appendix B Pseudospin Transformations

We show how to derive the matrices U𝒪U_{\mathcal{O}} for the space group generators and U𝒯U_{\mathcal{T}} for time-reversal. The transformation of the pseudospin under a space group generator can be deduced by first performing the active transformation on the pseudospin and then changing the local coordinates due to sublattice mixing. The representations of the generators C¯6\overline{C}_{6} and SS acting on a pseudospin state |±⟩μ|\pm\rangle_{\mu} on sublattice μ\mu are

RC¯6,μ\displaystyle R_{\overline{C}_{6},\mu} =exp(−i2​π3𝒏^C¯6,μ⋅𝑱)\displaystyle=\exp\left(-i\frac{2\pi}{3}\bm{\hat{n}}_{\overline{C}_{6},\mu}\cdot\bm{J}\right) (35a)
RS,μ\displaystyle R_{S,\mu} =exp(−iπ𝒏^S,μ⋅𝑱)\displaystyle=\exp\left(-i\pi\bm{\hat{n}}_{S,\mu}\cdot\bm{J}\right) (35b)

where 𝒏^𝒪,μ\bm{\hat{n}}_{{\mathcal{O}},\mu} is the rotation axis of the generator 𝒪{\mathcal{O}} written in the local frame μ\mu and 𝑱\bm{J} is the angular momentum operator. For the ground state (4), we have J=4J=4, but we note it is equivalent and simpler computationally to take the ground state doublet as |±⟩=|m=±1⟩|\pm\rangle=|m=\pm 1\rangle with J=1J=1 [47]. In global Cartesian coordinates,

𝒏^C¯6=13​(1,1,1)global,𝒏^S=12​(1,1,0)global.\bm{\hat{n}}_{\overline{C}_{6}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(1,1,1)_{\textrm{global}},\quad\bm{\hat{n}}_{S}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1,1,0)_{\textrm{global}}. (36)

Since the local frames differ on each sublattice, we define S​O​(3)SO(3) matrices Oμ→νO_{\mu\to\nu} which map the local frame μ\mu to the local frame ν\nu by

Oμ→ν\displaystyle O_{\mu\to\nu} =Wν​Wμ⊺\displaystyle=W_{\nu}W_{\mu}^{\intercal} (37)

where the columns of WμW_{\mu} are the local frame basis vectors (x^μ,y^μ,z^μ)(\hat{x}_{\mu},\hat{y}_{\mu},\hat{z}_{\mu}). We call the unitary matrices representing these rotations Rμ→νR_{\mu\to\nu}. Putting it together,

U𝒪,μ\displaystyle U_{{\mathcal{O}},\mu} =𝒫​Rμ→𝒪⁡(μ)​R𝒪,μ​𝒫\displaystyle=\mathcal{P}R_{\mu\to{\mathcal{O}}(\mu)}R_{{\mathcal{O}},\mu}\mathcal{P} (38)

where 𝒫\mathcal{P} is the projection to the ground state doublet. Evaluating (38) explicitly, the matrices U𝒪,μU_{{\mathcal{O}},\mu} are independent of the sublattice index, and are given in Eqs. (22b-22d).

For the time reversal operator 𝒯=exp⁡(i​π​Jy)​𝒦\mathcal{T}=\exp\left(i\pi J^{y}\right)\mathcal{K}, the matrix U𝒯U_{\mathcal{T}} evaluates explicitly to

U𝒯\displaystyle U_{\mathcal{T}} =𝒫​exp⁡(i​π​Jy)​𝒫\displaystyle=\mathcal{P}\exp\left(i\pi J^{y}\right)\mathcal{P} (39a)
=(0110).\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}. (39b)

Appendix C Constraints on the Mean-Field Amplitudes

On the pyrochlore lattice, all nearest-neighbour bonds are symmetry-related. In this work, we will always take (i0,j0)=(𝟎0,𝟎1)(i_{0},j_{0})=(\bm{0}_{0},\bm{0}_{1}) as the reference bond and denote it by (0,1)(0,1) for brevity. This lets us express all ui​jγu^{\gamma}_{ij} in terms of u01γu^{\gamma}_{01}, corresponding to the reference bond.

We demand that the gauge-enriched symmetry operations 𝒪~=𝒢𝒪∘𝒪\tilde{{\mathcal{O}}}={\mathcal{G}}_{\mathcal{O}}\circ{\mathcal{O}} be symmetries of HMFH_{\textrm{MF}};

u𝒪​i,𝒪​jh\displaystyle u^{h}_{{\mathcal{O}}i,{\mathcal{O}}j} =U𝒪​ui​jh​U𝒪†​ei⁡(−ϕ𝒪​[𝒪​i]+ϕ𝒪​[𝒪​j])\displaystyle=U_{\mathcal{O}}u^{h}_{ij}U_{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}e^{i(-\phi_{\mathcal{O}}[{\mathcal{O}}i]+\phi_{\mathcal{O}}[{\mathcal{O}}j])} (40a)
u𝒪​i,𝒪​jp\displaystyle u^{p}_{{\mathcal{O}}i,{\mathcal{O}}j} =U𝒪∗​ui​jp​U𝒪†​ei⁡(ϕ𝒪​[𝒪​i]+ϕ𝒪​[𝒪​j])\displaystyle=U_{\mathcal{O}}^{*}u^{p}_{ij}U_{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}e^{i(\phi_{\mathcal{O}}[{\mathcal{O}}i]+\phi_{\mathcal{O}}[{\mathcal{O}}j])} (40b)

where ϕ𝒪\phi_{\mathcal{O}} are the phase factors from the PSG solution (23). The phases ϕ𝒪\phi_{\mathcal{O}} do not depend on the choice of ground state doublet, but the transformation matrices U𝒪U_{\mathcal{O}} do. Defining the vectors

ti​jγ\displaystyle t^{\gamma}_{ij} =(ai​jγbi​jγci​jγdi​jγ)⊺\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}a^{\gamma}_{ij}&b^{\gamma}_{ij}&c^{\gamma}_{ij}&d^{\gamma}_{ij}\end{pmatrix}^{\intercal} (41)

where γ∈{h,p}\gamma\in\{h,p\} indicates hopping or pairing, the PSG constraints can be rewritten as

t𝒪​i,𝒪​jγ\displaystyle t^{\gamma}_{{\mathcal{O}}i,{\mathcal{O}}j} =ℛ𝒪γ​ti​jγ\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}^{\gamma}_{\mathcal{O}}t^{\gamma}_{ij} (42)

where the O⁡(4)O(4) matrices ℛ𝒪γ\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{O}}^{\gamma} are determined by U𝒪U_{\mathcal{O}} and the phase factors in Eqs. (40a-40b). This shows that it is enough to specify ui​jγu^{\gamma}_{ij} on a single bond (i0,j0)(i_{0},j_{0}) to determine all the remaining ui​jγu^{\gamma}_{ij}.Finally, since we have specialized to ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquids, the phases are either 11 or −1-1, so (ℛ𝒪γ)∗=ℛ𝒪γ(\mathcal{R}^{\gamma}_{\mathcal{O}})^{*}=\mathcal{R}^{\gamma}_{\mathcal{O}}.

Defining the vector 𝒕i​j=(ti​jh,ti​jp)∈ℂ8\bm{t}_{ij}=(t^{h}_{ij},t^{p}_{ij})\in\mathbb{C}^{8}, the transformation law (42) becomes

𝒕i​j\displaystyle\bm{t}_{ij} =Ri​j​𝒕01\displaystyle=R_{ij}\bm{t}_{01} (43)

where the block-diagonal matrix Ri​j∈ℝ8×8R_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{8\times 8} is

Ri​j\displaystyle R_{ij} =(ℛi​jh𝟎4×4𝟎4×4ℛi​jp).\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{R}^{h}_{ij}&\mathbf{0}_{4\times 4}\\ \mathbf{0}_{4\times 4}&\mathcal{R}^{p}_{ij}\end{pmatrix}. (44)

Demanding that the gauge-enriched time reversal operation (21) is a symmetry of the mean-field Hamiltonian leads to the conditions

ui​jp\displaystyle u^{p}_{ij} =U𝒯∗​[ui​jp]∗​U𝒯†\displaystyle=U_{\mathcal{T}}^{*}\left[u^{p}_{ij}\right]^{*}U_{\mathcal{T}}^{\dagger} (45a)

(ah,bh,ch,dh)\displaystyle(a^{h},b^{h},c^{h},d^{h}) =((ah)∗,(bh)∗,(ch)∗,−(dh)∗)\displaystyle=((a^{h})^{*},(b^{h})^{*},(c^{h})^{*},-(d^{h})^{*}) (46a)
(ap,bp,cp,dp)\displaystyle(a^{p},b^{p},c^{p},d^{p}) =(−(ap)∗,−(bp)∗,−(cp)∗,(dp)∗),\displaystyle=(-(a^{p})^{*},-(b^{p})^{*},-(c^{p})^{*},(d^{p})^{*}), (46b)

which hold for every bond (i,j)(i,j). Thus, ah,bh,ch,dpa^{h},b^{h},c^{h},d^{p} are real and ap,bp,cp,dha^{p},b^{p},c^{p},d^{h} are imaginary.

The last set of constraints arises because a bond can be mapped to itself in several inequivalent ways [20]. First, we note that the hopping and pairing mean-field amplitudes satisfy the following symmetry properties

χj​i\displaystyle\chi_{ji} =χi​j∗\displaystyle=\chi^{*}_{ij} (47a)

Δj​i\displaystyle\Delta_{ji} =−Δi​j\displaystyle=-\Delta_{ij} (47c)

which follows from the definitions (12a-12d). A group theory analysis [20] shows that

g1\displaystyle g_{1} =id\displaystyle=\mathrm{id} (48a)

Applying Eqs. (40a-40b) with the stabilizers above and the properties (47a-47d), we find

(ah,bh,ch,dh)\displaystyle(a^{h},b^{h},c^{h},d^{h}) =(−1)nC​S×(ah,bh,−ch,−dh)\displaystyle=(-1)^{n_{CS}}\times(a^{h},b^{h},-c^{h},-d^{h}) (49a)

=(−1)n1+nC+nS​T​(ap,−bp,cp,dp),\displaystyle=(-1)^{n_{1}+n_{C}+n_{ST}}(a^{p},-b^{p},c^{p},d^{p}), (50b)

{ap=bp=0if ​n1+nC+nS​T≡0(mod2)ap=cp=dp=0if ​n1+nC+nS​T≡1(mod2)\displaystyle\begin{cases}a^{p}=b^{p}=0&\textrm{if }n_{1}+n_{C}+n_{ST}\equiv 0\pmod{2}\\ a^{p}=c^{p}=d^{p}=0&\textrm{if }n_{1}+n_{C}+n_{ST}\equiv 1\pmod{2}\end{cases} (51)

and ah,bh∈ℝa^{h},b^{h}\in\mathbb{R} are the nonzero hopping terms.

Appendix E Self-Consistent Equations

E.1 The Standard Approach and Its Issues

We summarize the usual argument to derive the self-consistent equations. After mean-field decoupling, the Hamiltonian (13) is

HMF\displaystyle H_{\textrm{MF}} =−∑⟨i​j⟩(𝑩i​j†ξi​j𝓐i​j+𝓐i​j†ξi​j𝑩i​j−𝓐i​j†ξi​j𝓐i​j)\displaystyle=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}(\bm{B}_{ij}^{\dagger}\xi_{ij}\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{ij}+\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}^{\dagger}_{ij}\xi_{ij}\bm{B}_{ij}-\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}^{\dagger}_{ij}\xi_{ij}\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{ij}) (54)

where 𝑩i​j\bm{B}_{ij} and 𝓐i​j\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{ij} are defined in section III.2. One can find the self-consistent equations by treating all mean-field amplitudes 𝓐i​j\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{ij} as independent and then minimizing the mean-field energy

⟨HMF⟩\displaystyle\langle H_{\textrm{MF}}\rangle =−∑⟨i​j⟩(𝑿i​j†ξi​j𝓐i​j+𝓐i​j†ξi​j𝑿i​j−𝓐i​j†ξi​j𝓐i​j).\displaystyle=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}(\bm{X}_{ij}^{\dagger}\xi_{ij}\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{ij}+\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}^{\dagger}_{ij}\xi_{ij}\bm{X}_{ij}-\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}^{\dagger}_{ij}\xi_{ij}\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{ij}). (55)

For brevity, we have denoted the expectation value of the vector 𝑩\bm{B} by 𝑿\bm{X}. Then,

∂⟨HMF⟩∂𝓐k​ℓ†=0\displaystyle\frac{\partial\langle H_{\textrm{MF}}\rangle}{\partial\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}^{\dagger}_{k\ell}}=0 ⇔ξk​ℓ​(𝑿k​ℓ−𝓐k​ℓ)=0\displaystyle\iff\xi_{k\ell}(\bm{X}_{k\ell}-\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{k\ell})=0 (56a)
⇔𝑿k​ℓ=𝓐k​ℓ\displaystyle\iff\bm{X}_{k\ell}=\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{k\ell} (56b)

provided ξk​ℓ\xi_{k\ell} is invertible. We call Eq. (56b) the “naive self-consistent equations”, which holds for all bonds (k,ℓ)(k,\ell). In the notation of previous work such as [20], Eq. (56b) reads

⟨A^k​ℓ⟩\displaystyle\langle\hat{A}_{k\ell}\rangle =Ak​ℓ.\displaystyle=A_{k\ell}. (57)

Once (56b) is satisfied, we have

⟨HMF⟩|consistent\displaystyle\langle H_{\textrm{MF}}\rangle\big|_{\textrm{consistent}} =−∑⟨i​j⟩𝓐i​j†ξi​j𝓐i​j.\displaystyle=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{ij}^{\dagger}\xi_{ij}\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{ij}. (58)

Now, we would like to impose PSG constraints on the ansatz. As argued in the main text, this can modify the form of the self-consistent equations beacuse the symmetries of the ansatz mean that the amplitudes on each bond are no longer independent. If the ansatz respects the PSG, there are only a few independent mean-field amplitudes (say, the set of A01A_{01} for all A^\hat{A}), and the remaining Ai​jA_{ij} can depend on them in nontrivial ways. Therefore, one should apply the PSG constraints to the ansatz first and then minimize the energy with respect to the independent mean-field amplitudes. It can happen that the two approaches are equivalent if the decoupling and PSG constraints are simple enough, as was the case in the previously studied dipolar-octupolar model [20].

An analogy can be used to illustrate this point: consider the constrained optimization problem

minimize f⁡(x,y)=x2+y2\displaystyle f(x,y)=x^{2}+y^{2}
subject to g⁡(x,y)=y−x−1=0\displaystyle g(x,y)=y-x-1=0

where x,y∈ℝx,y\in\mathbb{R}. In this analogy, ff corresponds to ⟨HMF⟩\langle H_{\textrm{MF}}\rangle and gg corresponds to the PSG constraints. The equations to be solved to determine the minimum correspond to the self-consistent equations. If we minimized ff first and then applied the constraint, we would find (x,y)=(0,0)(x,y)=(0,0), which does not satisfy the constraint. So we fail to find any solutions. The “self-consistent equations” in this case are

∂f⁡(x,y)∂x\displaystyle\frac{\partial f(x,y)}{\partial x} =0\displaystyle=0 (59a)
∂f⁡(x,y)∂y\displaystyle\frac{\partial f(x,y)}{\partial y} =0.\displaystyle=0. (59b)

On the other hand, if we applied the constraint first (by solving for yy as a function of xx) and then minimized with respect to xx, we would get

f⁡(x,y⁡(x))=x2+(x+1)2f(x,y(x))=x^{2}+(x+1)^{2}

which has a minimum at x=−12x=-\frac{1}{2}. Thus, the minimum occurs at (x,y)=(−12,12)(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}), which is the correct solution to the constrained optimization problem. The “self-consistent equation” in this case is

∂f⁡(x,y⁡(x))∂x\displaystyle\frac{\partial f(x,y(x))}{\partial x} =0,\displaystyle=0, (60)

and we see that Eqs. (59a) and (59b) are not the same as (60). This is to be expected because the first approach does not actually work in general, as the above example shows. However, if the constraint was instead g⁡(x,y)=y−xg(x,y)=y-x, then the first approach still works. This is only because we got lucky with the specific constraint. Thus, we are led to suspect that the self-consistent equations are not always (56b).

In appendix E.1, we defined vectors of expectation values 𝑿\bm{X}. Here, it is clearer to separate 𝑿\bm{X} into two halves, 𝑿=(Xh,Xp)\bm{X}=(X^{h},X^{p}) where the 44-component vectors XγX^{\gamma} have components

[Xi​jh]α\displaystyle[X^{h}_{ij}]^{\alpha} =⟨𝑩i†​σα​𝑩j⟩\displaystyle=\langle\bm{B}^{\dagger}_{i}\sigma^{\alpha}\bm{B}_{j}\rangle (61a)
[Xi​jp]α\displaystyle[X^{p}_{ij}]^{\alpha} =⟨𝑩i​(i​σy​σα)​𝑩j⟩.\displaystyle=\langle\bm{B}_{i}(i\sigma^{y}\sigma^{\alpha})\bm{B}_{j}\rangle. (61b)

X𝒪​i,𝒪​jγ\displaystyle X^{\gamma}_{{\mathcal{O}}i,{\mathcal{O}}j} =ℛ𝒪γ​Xi​jγ,\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}^{\gamma}_{\mathcal{O}}X^{\gamma}_{ij}, (64)

which is structurally the same as Eq. (42). Equivalently, the transformation law is

𝑿i​j\displaystyle\bm{X}_{ij} =Ri​j​𝑿01.\displaystyle=R_{ij}\bm{X}_{01}. (65)

E.3 The Role of the Decoupling

The previous two subsections have been independent of any details of the mean-field decoupling; that is, the matrix ξi​j\xi_{ij} in Eq. (13). We found that the transformation of the ti​jγt^{\gamma}_{ij} and Xi​jγX^{\gamma}_{ij} only depends on the PSG, and not the decoupling used. Here, we will see that the decoupling only affects how the mean-field amplitudes Ai​jA_{ij} transform. A general mean-field decoupling will relate 𝒕\bm{t} to 𝓐\bm{{\mathcal{A}}} in the following way:

𝒕i​j\displaystyle\bm{t}_{ij} =ξi​j​𝓐i​j∗\displaystyle=\xi_{ij}\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{ij}^{*} (66)

where ξi​j∈ℝ8×8\xi_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{8\times 8} is precisely the symmetric matrix introduced in Eq. (13). This follows from the definition of the tγt^{\gamma} vectors and the bond operators. For example, the singlet hopping term ξi​jχ,χ​χi​j∗​χ^i​j\xi^{\chi,\chi}_{ij}\chi^{*}_{ij}\hat{\chi}_{ij} in HMFH_{\textrm{MF}} corresponds to

ai​jh\displaystyle a^{h}_{ij} =ξi​jχ,χ​χi​j∗\displaystyle=\xi^{\chi,\chi}_{ij}\chi^{*}_{ij} (67)

because

𝑩i†​(ai​jh​𝟙𝟚×𝟚)​𝔹𝕛\displaystyle\bm{B}_{i}^{\ \dagger}(a^{h}_{ij}\openone_{2\times 2})\bm{B}_{j} =ai​jh​χ^i​j.\displaystyle=a^{h}_{ij}\hat{\chi}_{ij}. (68)

Since we have specialized to Hamiltonians of the form (8), each pseudospin bilinear Siα​SjβS^{\alpha}_{i}S^{\beta}_{j} contains two b†b^{\dagger} operators and two bb operators. Thus, ξ\xi takes the block-diagonal form

ξi​j\displaystyle\xi_{ij} =(Li​jh𝟎4×4𝟎4×4Li​jp),\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}L^{h}_{ij}&\mathbf{0}_{4\times 4}\\ \mathbf{0}_{4\times 4}&L^{p}_{ij}\end{pmatrix}, (69)

where Li​jγ∈ℝ4×4L^{\gamma}_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times 4} are real symmetric matrices. They must be real-valued and symmetric to ensure that HMFH_{\textrm{MF}} is Hermitian. We can use the transformation properties of 𝒕i​j\bm{t}_{ij} from appendix E.2 to deduce the transformation properties of 𝓐i​j\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{ij}. We have that

ξi​j​𝓐i​j∗\displaystyle\xi_{ij}\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{ij}^{*} =𝒕i​j\displaystyle=\bm{t}_{ij}
=Ri​j​𝒕01\displaystyle=R_{ij}\bm{t}_{01}
=Ri​j​ξ01​𝓐01∗,\displaystyle=R_{ij}\xi_{01}\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{01}^{*}, (70)

from which it follows that

𝓐i​j\displaystyle\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{ij} =Si​j​𝓐01\displaystyle=S_{ij}\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{01} (71)

where

Si​j\displaystyle S_{ij} =ξi​j−1​Ri​j∗​ξ01\displaystyle=\xi^{-1}_{ij}R^{*}_{ij}\xi_{01} (72)
=([Li​jh]−1​ℛi​jh​L01h𝟎4×4𝟎4×4[Li​jp]−1​ℛi​jp​L01p).\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}[L^{h}_{ij}]^{-1}\mathcal{R}^{h}_{ij}L^{h}_{01}&\mathbf{0}_{4\times 4}\\ \mathbf{0}_{4\times 4}&[L^{p}_{ij}]^{-1}\mathcal{R}^{p}_{ij}L^{p}_{01}\end{pmatrix}.

For the PSG classes we will study, the ℛγ\mathcal{R}^{\gamma} matrices are real-valued, so Ri​j∗=Ri​jR^{*}_{ij}=R_{ij}. We see that 𝓐i​j\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{ij} depends linearly on 𝓐01\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{01}.

E.4 The Generalized Self-Consistent Equations

To derive the general self-consistent equations, we proceed as outlined in appendix E.1; write all amplitudes and expectation values as functions of the reference bonds, and then minimize with respect to the independent amplitudes:

0\displaystyle 0 =∂⟨HMF⟩∂𝓐01†\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\langle H_{\textrm{MF}}\rangle}{\partial\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{01}^{\dagger}} (73a)
=∑⟨i​j⟩∂𝓐i​j†∂𝓐01†​ξi​j​(𝑿i​j−𝓐i​j)\displaystyle=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\frac{\partial\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}^{\dagger}_{ij}}{\partial\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{01}^{\dagger}}\xi_{ij}(\bm{X}_{ij}-\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{ij}) (73b)

Appendix F Explicit Expressions for Mean-Field Calculations

F.1 Fourier Transformation of the Mean-Field Hamiltonian

The Fourier transform of the spinon operator is

b𝒓μ,α\displaystyle b_{{{\bm{r}}}_{\mu},\alpha} =1Nuc​∑𝒌∈BZb𝒌,μ,α​ei​𝒌⋅𝒓,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{\textrm{uc}}}}\sum_{{{\bm{k}}}\in\textrm{BZ}}b_{{{\bm{k}}},\mu,\alpha}e^{i{{\bm{k}}}\cdot{{\bm{r}}}}, (88)

where NucN_{\textrm{uc}} is the number of unit cells, BZ denotes the first Brillouin zone, and we use the convention that the exponential factor only depends on the unit cell position 𝒓{{\bm{r}}}, not on the sublattice. In terms of the vector Ψ𝒌=(𝒃𝒌,0,⋯𝒃𝒌,3,𝒃−𝒌,0†,⋯𝒃−𝒌,3†)⊺\Psi_{{\bm{k}}}=\begin{pmatrix}\bm{b}_{{{\bm{k}}},0},&\cdots&\bm{b}_{{{\bm{k}}},3},\bm{b}^{\dagger}_{-{{\bm{k}}},0},&\cdots&\bm{b}^{\dagger}_{-{{\bm{k}}},3}\end{pmatrix}^{\intercal}, the mean-field Hamiltonian (17) becomes

HMF\displaystyle H_{\textrm{MF}} =∑𝒌∈BZΨ𝒌†​ℋ​(𝒌)​Ψ𝒌\displaystyle=\sum_{{{\bm{k}}}\in\textrm{BZ}}\Psi^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}}}\mathcal{H}({{\bm{k}}})\Psi_{{\bm{k}}}
−4​Nuc​λ​(1+κ)+Nuc​E0\displaystyle-4N_{\textrm{uc}}\lambda(1+\kappa)+N_{\textrm{uc}}E_{0} (89)

where E0E_{0} is shorthand for the following sum over unit cell bonds:

E0\displaystyle E_{0} =∑⟨i​j⟩∈uc𝓐i​j†​ξi​j​𝓐i​j.\displaystyle=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle\in\textrm{uc}}\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}^{\dagger}_{ij}\xi_{ij}\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{ij}. (90)

The 16×1616\times 16 matrix ℋ⁡(𝒌)\mathcal{H}({{\bm{k}}}) takes the standard Bogoliubov form

ℋ⁡(𝒌)\displaystyle\mathcal{H}({{\bm{k}}}) =(Hh​(𝒌)Hp​(𝒌)Hp†​(𝒌)Hh⊺​(−𝒌),)\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}H_{h}({{\bm{k}}})&H_{p}({{\bm{k}}})\\ H^{\dagger}_{p}({{\bm{k}}})&H^{\intercal}_{h}(-{{\bm{k}}}),\end{pmatrix} (91)

where we have defined

F.3 Evaluating Ground State Expectation Values

To solve the (generalized) self-consistent equations, we use an iterative algorithm. We start with a random ansatz 𝓐i0,j0(0)\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{i_{0},j_{0}}^{(0)} and fix a real number δ\delta, which is used in the convergence criterion. Step nn in the algorithm generates a new ansatz 𝓐i0,j0(n)\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{i_{0},j_{0}}^{(n)} and Lagrange multiplier λ(n)\lambda^{(n)}, which depend on 𝓐i0,j0(n−1)\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{i_{0},j_{0}}^{(n-1)} and λ(n−1)\lambda^{(n-1)}. In detail, step nn consists of the following:

  1. 1.

    Solve for the Lagrange multiplier λ(n)\lambda^{(n)} using the self-consistency equation ⟨ni⟩=κ\langle n_{i}\rangle=\kappa. This can be done by bisection on the interval λ∈(|hmax|,5)\lambda\in(|h_{\textrm{max}}|,5) where hmaxh_{\textrm{max}} is the largest eigenvalue of HMFH_{\textrm{MF}} over the first Brillouin zone. For the values of κ,Jz​z,J±,J±⁣±\kappa,J_{zz},J_{\pm},J_{\pm\pm} considered in this work, it suffices to bound λ\lambda above by 55.

  2. 2.

    Using the values 𝓐i0,j0(n−1),λ(n)\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{i_{0},j_{0}}^{(n-1)},\lambda^{(n)} in HMFH_{\textrm{MF}}, compute the ground state expectation values 𝑿i0,j0(n)=⟨𝑩i0,j0⟩\bm{X}_{i_{0},j_{0}}^{(n)}=\langle\bm{B}_{i_{0},j_{0}}\rangle.

  3. 3.

    Update 𝓐i0,j0(n)=(W−1​V)​𝑿i0,j0(n)\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{i_{0},j_{0}}^{(n)}=(W^{-1}V)\bm{X}_{i_{0},j_{0}}^{(n)}.

  4. 4.

    Increment nn by one, return to step 1, and repeat until the desired convergence is achieved. Convergence is determined by the condition |𝓐i0,j0(n)−𝓐i0,j0(n−1)|<δ\left|\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{i_{0},j_{0}}^{(n)}-\bm{{\mathcal{A}}}_{i_{0},j_{0}}^{(n-1)}\right|<\delta.

At each step of this algorithm, it is necessary to evaluate ground state expectation values ⟨𝑩i0,j0⟩\langle\bm{B}_{i_{0},j_{0}}\rangle for the reference bond (i0,j0)=(𝟎0,𝟎1)(i_{0},j_{0})=(\bm{0}_{0},\bm{0}_{1}). For this calculation, it is convenient to write the Bogoliubov transformation matrix P⁡(𝒌)P({{\bm{k}}}) in terms of 8×88\times 8 submatrices

P⁡(𝒌)\displaystyle P({{\bm{k}}}) =(P11​(𝒌)P12​(𝒌)P21​(𝒌)P22​(𝒌)),\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}P_{11}({{\bm{k}}})&P_{12}({{\bm{k}}})\\ P_{21}({{\bm{k}}})&P_{22}({{\bm{k}}})\end{pmatrix}, (99)

where the blocks satisfy

P22​(𝒌)=P11∗​(−𝒌),P21​(𝒌)=P12∗​(−𝒌)P_{22}({{\bm{k}}})=P_{11}^{*}(-{{\bm{k}}}),\quad P_{21}({{\bm{k}}})=P_{12}^{*}(-{{\bm{k}}}) (100)

due to the structure of the matrix ℋ⁡(𝒌)\mathcal{H}({{\bm{k}}}) [39]. We can then write the Bogoliubov transformation (94) as
